title: Motion in a Plane (2D & 3D Kinematics)
subtitle: Zero-to-JEE-Advanced Visual Textbook: Vector Resolution, Projectile Motion (Ground, Inclined Plane, Tower), 2D Relative Motion (River-Boat, Rain-Man) & Circular Kinematics
introduction:
💡 First-Time Reader Intuition: Moving in Two Dimensions

In Chapter 02, we restricted a particle's motion to a single straight line ($x$-axis). But in the real world, objects move across floors, curve through the sky, or orbit in space—requiring two ($x, y$) or three ($x, y, z$) coordinates simultaneously.

The Independence of Perpendicular Motions (Galileo's Principle):
When a projectile moves in a vertical plane, its horizontal motion and vertical motion are completely independent of each other! Horizontal velocity remains constant (if air drag is ignored), while vertical motion behaves exactly like free fall under constant gravity $g$.

topics.title: Ground-to-Ground Projectile Motion: Time of Flight, Range, Max Height & Trajectory Equation
topics.theoryHtml:
1.1 Resolution of Initial Velocity & The 4 Master Projectile Formulas
Setup:
A particle is projected from the origin $(0,0)$ with initial speed $u$ at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal. Choose origin at launch point, rightward as $+x$, upward as $+y$.
$$\text{Initial Velocity Components:} \qquad u_x = u\cos\theta \quad (a_x = 0), \qquad u_y = u\sin\theta \quad (a_y = -g)$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{1. Time of Flight } (T): & \quad \boxed{T = \frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}} \\[6pt] \text{2. Maximum Height } (H): & \quad \boxed{H = \frac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}} \\[6pt] \text{3. Horizontal Range } (R): & \quad \boxed{R = \frac{u^2\sin(2\theta)}{g}} \\[6pt] \text{4. Equation of Trajectory:} & \quad \boxed{y = x\tan\theta - \frac{gx^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta} = x\tan\theta\left(1 - \frac{x}{R}\right)} \end{aligned}$$
1.2 Complementary Angles & Max Range Properties
  • 1. Complementary Angles ($+\theta$ and $90^\circ - \theta$):
    Projecting at angle $\theta$ and at angle $90^\circ - \theta$ with the same speed $u$ yields the exact same horizontal range $R$! The maximum heights for these two angles ($H_1$ and $H_2$) satisfy the geometric mean rule:
    $$\boxed{R = 4\sqrt{H_1 H_2}}$$
  • 2. Maximum Possible Range ($R_{\max}$):
    Since $\sin(2\theta)$ reaches its maximum value of $1$ at $2\theta = 90^\circ \implies \theta = 45^\circ$:
    $$\boxed{R_{\max} = \frac{u^2}{g} = 2H_{\max} \quad (\text{at } \theta = 45^\circ)}$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation of Projectile Formulas

1. Time of Flight ($T$): Set vertical displacement $y = 0$ in $y = u_y t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$:

$$0 = (u\sin\theta)T - \frac{1}{2}gT^2 \implies T = \frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$$

2. Horizontal Range ($R$): Multiply horizontal speed $u_x = u\cos\theta$ by total flight time $T$:

$$R = (u\cos\theta)\left(\frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}\right) = \frac{u^2(2\sin\theta\cos\theta)}{g} = \frac{u^2\sin(2\theta)}{g}$$

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Minimum Speed at Highest Point): At maximum height $H_{\max}$, vertical velocity is $v_y = 0$. However, horizontal velocity $v_x = u\cos\theta$ remains unchanged and non-zero (unless projected straight up at $90^\circ$). Therefore, speed at the peak is not zero—it is $u\cos\theta$!

topics.title: Projectile on an Inclined Plane (Up-the-Plane and Down-the-Plane Formulas)
topics.theoryHtml:
2.1 Setup & Accelerated Axes Parallel/Perpendicular to Incline
Smart Coordinate Rotation:
Instead of tilting your head to use horizontal/vertical axes, tilt your coordinate system so the $x'$-axis runs parallel up the incline and the $y'$-axis runs perpendicular upward from the incline!
In this tilted frame, acceleration due to gravity $g$ resolves into two components:
  • Parallel down the incline: $a_x = -g\sin\alpha$
  • Perpendicular into the incline: $a_y = -g\cos\alpha$
$$\textbf{Time of Flight on Incline (Up the Plane at angle } \alpha \text{, launch angle } \theta \text{ to incline):} \quad \boxed{T = \frac{2u\sin\theta}{g\cos\alpha}}$$
$$\textbf{Maximum Range Up the Incline:} \qquad \boxed{R_{\max} = \frac{u^2}{g(1 + \sin\alpha)} \quad \left(\text{at launch angle } \theta = 45^\circ - \frac{\alpha}{2}\right)}$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation of Time of Flight on Incline

Set perpendicular displacement $y' = 0$ using $y' = u_y' t - \frac{1}{2}a_y t^2$ where $u_y' = u\sin\theta$ and $a_y = g\cos\alpha$:

$$0 = (u\sin\theta)T - \frac{1}{2}(g\cos\alpha)T^2 \implies \boxed{T = \frac{2u\sin\theta}{g\cos\alpha}}$$

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Launch Angle Definition): In incline problems, angle $\theta$ is almost always measured relative to the incline surface, NOT relative to the horizontal ground!

topics.title: 2D Relative Motion: River-Crossing Boat Problems & Rain-Man Vector Relations
topics.theoryHtml:
3.1 River-Crossing Boat Master Formulas (Width $d$, River Speed $v_r$, Boat Speed in Still Water $v_b$)
Objective / ConditionFormulaKey Physics Insight
1. Minimum Time to Cross River ($t_{\min}$)$t_{\min} = \frac{d}{v_b}$ (at $\theta = 90^\circ$ across)To cross fastest, point the boat directly straight across ($90^\circ$ to bank). Drift is unavoidable!
2. Minimum Drift ($x_{\min} = 0$, Straight Across)$\sin\theta = \frac{v_r}{v_b}$ (upstream at angle $\theta$)Possible ONLY if $v_b > v_r$. If $v_b \le v_r$, zero drift is impossible!
3.2 Rain-Man Vector Relations
$$\vec{v}_{rm} = \vec{v}_r - \vec{v}_m \implies \vec{v}_r = \vec{v}_{rm} + \vec{v}_m$$

To keep dry, the man must hold his umbrella pointing parallel to the direction of apparent rain velocity $\vec{v}_{rm}$ as seen from his moving frame.
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation of Minimum Drift Condition

Let boat head upstream at angle $\theta$ with the straight-across line. Effective velocity along river flow is $v_x = v_r - v_b\sin\theta$. Setting drift to zero ($v_x = 0$):

$$\sin\theta = \frac{v_r}{v_b} \quad (\text{requires } v_b > v_r)$$

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Zero Drift with $v_b \le v_r$): If river speed $v_r = 5\text{ m/s}$ and swimmer speed $v_b = 3\text{ m/s}$, setting $\sin\theta = 5/3 > 1$ is mathematically impossible. Zero drift cannot be achieved!

topics.title: Circular Kinematics & Dynamics: Angular Variables, Centripetal Acceleration, Tangential Accel. & Banking of Roads
topics.theoryHtml:
4.1 Angular Variables & Radial/Tangential Acceleration
$$\theta = \frac{s}{r}, \qquad \omega = \frac{d\theta}{dt}, \qquad \alpha = \frac{d\omega}{dt}, \qquad v = r\omega$$
$$\text{1. Centripetal (Radial) Acceleration:} \quad \boxed{a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} = r\omega^2} \quad (\text{always points toward center})$$
$$\text{2. Tangential Acceleration:} \quad \boxed{a_t = \frac{dv}{dt} = r\alpha} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{Net Accel: } a = \sqrt{a_c^2 + a_t^2}$$
4.2 Banking of Roads & Maximum Safe Turning Speed
$$\boxed{\tan\theta = \frac{v^2}{rg} \quad (\text{frictionless banked road})} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \boxed{v_{\max} = \sqrt{rg\left(\frac{\mu_s + \tan\theta}{1 - \mu_s\tan\theta}\right)}}$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation of Centripetal Acceleration $a_c = v^2/r$

Vector velocity rotates by angle $\theta$ while magnitude $v$ stays constant. Magnitude of change in velocity is $|\Delta\v| = 2v\sin(\theta/2) \approx v\theta$. Dividing by $\Delta t$ and taking limit gives $a_c = v\frac{d\theta}{dt} = v\omega = \frac{v^2}{r}$.

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Centrifugal Force): Centrifugal force ($mv^2/r$) is a pseudo force experienced only in a non-inertial rotating frame. In an inertial ground frame, only real inward centripetal forces exist!

conclusion: You have mastered Chapter 03: Motion in a Plane! You are now ready to combine forces and Newton's laws in Chapter 04.

questions.prompt: A projectile is fired with speed $50\text{ m/s}$ at an angle $37^\circ$ with the horizontal ($g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$). Find its time of flight and horizontal range.
The maximum range of a projectile on horizontal ground is $400\text{ m}$. What is the maximum height reached by it?
questions.explanation: $R_{\max} = \frac{u^2}{g} = 400\text{ m}$. Maximum height at $\theta = 45^\circ$ is $H_{\max} = \frac{u^2\sin^2(45^\circ)}{2g} = \frac{400}{4} = 100\text{ m}$.

questions.prompt: A swimmer wants to cross a river $500\text{ m}$ wide flowing at $3\text{ m/s}$. If his swimming speed in still water is $5\text{ m/s}$, what is the minimum time he takes to cross?
